newsitem.title: RUSSIA: Controversy fails to derail Russian Norilsk sale.
newsitem.headline: Controversy fails to derail Russian Norilsk sale.

text.p: A last-ditch bid by top government officials to halt the controversial sale of a controlling stake in Russian mining giant Norilsk Nickel failed on Tuesday, and the tender was won by a partner of commercial bank Uneximbank.

Dmitry Ushakov, chairman of the tender committee and deputy chairman of Uneximbank, said Svift bid 236.18 million Ecus ($250.1 million) for the Norilsk NKEL.RTS shares against 171 million by unknown Advanced Industrial Technologies.
"The Svift bid is higher than that of Advanced Industrial Technologies, and we therefore name the shareholding company Svift the winner of the contest," Ushakov told reporters.
The winner also has to invest $300 million in a gas deposit which will be used to fuel RAO Norilsky Nikel's main metals combine, plus pay off company debts worth about $70 million.
Committee and Uneximbank sources later confirmed Svift was linked to Uneximbank, the powerful commercial group headed by former first deputy prime minister Vladimir Potanin.
"Svift represents our interests, therefore I am very happy," said a senior Uneximbank source who asked not to be named.
"Svift is part of the Interrosprom group," added Sergei Molozhavy, deputy chairman of the State Property Committee, Russia's privatisation ministry. Interrosprom is part of the Uneximbank-MFK group.

The announcement comes after days of fierce lobbying among commercial and political factions hoping to derail the deal. Its critics have said the terms of the tender gave Uneximbank an unfair advantage and deprived Russia of potential revenues.
The heat on Uneximbank was turned up after it was named victor in Russia's last big privatisation deal, for a quarter stake in telecom holding company Svyazinvest late last month.
Uneximbank led the winning $1.875-billion consortium, prompting a storm of protest in Russian media.

Businessmen said to be part of the losing consortium in the Svyazinvest privatisation, Russia's biggest ever, were thought to be behind a fierce campaign against Uneximbank, channelled through their media interests.
Doubtless Uneximbank will be bracing itself for a similar onslaught in the wake of the Norilsk result.
Foreign observers dismissed the smear campaign as sour grapes, adding that the winner had made the highest bid.
The Norilsk sale was more controversial in that it apparently favoured Uneximbank far more than the Svyazinvest sale ever could, metal and equity analysts have have said.

Of the six tender committee members, three represented the government and three Uneximbank. But the key casting vote was held by the committee's chairman, who turned out to be none other than Uneximbank's Uzhakov himself.
Bank MFK (IFCI in English), the investment arm of Uneximbank, is also closely linked to MFK Moscow Partners, the official organier of the tender.
Opposition to the deal in the highest government circles kept Russia's investment community guessing to the very last.
Prime Minister Viktor Chernomyrdin on Monday ordered state representatives in the committee to suspend the sale.
Russia's top privatisation official Alfred Kokh joined him just hours before Tuesday's decision, urging them to vote for delaying the sale for an unspecified period.
Molozhavy, one of the state representatives, said they were powerless to stop the tender taking place.

"To stop the tender was impossible. We had no reason to doubt the legality of the tender -- it was in accordance with Russia's civil code," he said, adding that the final decision to go ahead with the sale was taken "literally today".
Uneximbank won control of the Norilsk stake in 1995 under a shares-for-loans swap with the government, but had to put the stake up for auction this year under the terms of the swap.

The bank has struggled to implement a rescue package for the mining monolith, which produces vast quantities of base and precious metals profitably, but shoulders the huge cost of supporting an entire city built around its flagship combine.
It is the world's biggest palladium producer, could become the number one nickel supplier this year, and is also an important supplier of platinum, copper and cobalt.
The Norilsk and Svyazinvest sales are part of the latest round of big state sell-offs in Russia expected to raise $4-5 billion for state coffers in 1997 alone.
The next big test for the Kremlin, already under pressure to make privatisation fairer, could well be the sale of 51 percent of state oil firm Rosneft, pencilled in for September.
